papers.title: Tn-Seq-based identification of genes that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates
papers.abstract: Microbial biofilms, whether surface-associated or in the form of aggregated microbes, cause a variety of persistent infections due to their inherent tolerance to antibiotic treatment. Current knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance is fragmented, and the relative importance of previously identified factors remains unknown. We developed a Tn-Seq-based workflow that enables simultaneous assessment of the relative antibiotic tolerance of thousands of individual clonal bacterial aggregates, each established by a single transposon mutant. Using this genome-wide Tn-Seq analysis approach, we identified several factors and pathways that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates. The majority of these factors are important for aggregate-associated tolerance to specific antibiotics, whereas some factors play a role in aggregate-associated tolerance regardless of the class of antibiotic. This methodology provides a framework that can be adapted to investigate aggregate-associated tolerance for other bacterial species and in response to different antimicrobial agents and stressors.

papers.title: Particle-Associated Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
papers.abstract: Free-living and particle-associated bacteria play distinct roles in the cycling of organic matter, but how these lifestyles are partitioned in the highly productive, rapidly warming Bering and Chukchi Seas is largely unknown. During the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, a period of anomalously warm sea surface temperatures, we collected 78 samples at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) at 12 process stations and sequentially filtered them onto 20 {micro}m, 3 {micro}m, and 0.2 {micro}m filters. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances, we resolved four sample clusters. Although pore size was not used to build the clusters, communities separated into a free-living cluster associated mainly with Anadyr Water (FL1; 0.2 {micro}m fraction) and three particle-associated clusters (PA1-PA3; 3 and 20 {micro}m fractions), several of which were enriched in Bacteroidia. Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia were present in all size fractions, with Gammaproteobacteria most biased toward the free-living fraction. Community structure did not differ with depth, consistent with the shallow, weakly stratified shelf, and distance-based redundancy analysis identified salinity as the sole significant environmental factor distinguishing communities. These results suggest that lifestyle and water-mass origin, rather than depth, structure size-fractionated bacterial communities on the Pacific Arctic shelf, and that freshening and changes in bloom dynamics could reshape particle-associated communities in this region.

papers.title: Factors affecting microbial community composition in Split Lake, MB, Canada
papers.abstract: Split Lake is a large freshwater lake in northern Manitoba, Canada, that receives major inflows from the Nelson River, Burntwood River, and Grassy River. In 1976, during the Churchill River Diversion (CRD) project, most of the water in the Churchill River was diverted into the Nelson River via the Rat River, and the Burntwood River, creating a large inflow pressure in the lower Nelson area, including Split Lake. Decades after its implementation, the Churchill River Diversion still influences ecological and environmental processes in the area. In this study, metabarcoding of the 16S rRNA gene was employed to characterize the microbial community structure of the lake. Environmental factors (temperature, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen) and cyanotoxin levels were also assessed. The objectives of this study were to establish a baseline for microbiota across the lake and examine how environmental variables affect microbial population dynamics. The study was conducted in the summer of 2024, encompassing 14 sites on Split Lake and 2 sites on Assean Lake, an adjacent waterbody with minimal influence from hydroelectric infrastructure. Split Lake was found to harbor six distinct microbial clusters, with turbidity and dissolved oxygen levels correlating with different aquatic regimes within the lake. The predominant taxa in Split Lake included Actinobacteria hgcI clade and Cyanobium. Microcystin concentrations measured throughout the study were always below the Maximum Acceptable Concentration (MAC) set for Canadian federal drinking water standards.

papers.title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
papers.abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.

papers.title: Intrinsic timekeeping in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks allow organisms to anticipate predictable environmental changes across the day-night cycle. Here we show that the bacterium Escherichia coli exhibits intrinsic timekeeping that anticipates daily temperature cycles. E. coli biofilms entrained to daily temperature shifts, producing 24-hour rhythms in curli plaque formation that persisted under constant temperature. Mechanistically, genetic analyses localized the autonomous timing machinery to the Rcs phosphorelay, which exhibits structural and conceptual parallels with other circadian systems. The BluFR sensory pathway, which acts upstream of the Rcs phosphorelay, linked temperature and blue-light cycles to rhythmic curli production. Flagellar promoter activity and curli production peaked at opposite times of day, suggesting daily coordination of adhesion and motility programs. These findings identify an intrinsic timing system in E. coli that expands our understanding of biological timekeeping.

papers.title: A large, distinct family of RNase H fold nucleases associated with numerous defense systems in prokaryotes
papers.abstract: During the last decade, systematic efforts aimed at the characterization of prokaryotic immunity resulted in the discovery of several hundred distinct defense systems in bacteria and archaea. This suggests that the common defense systems were already known and only rare ones remained to be identified. Here we present a genomic census and analysis of a vast family of bacterial and archaeal proteins (known as Domain of Unknown Function, DUF3800) that contain a distinct variant of the RNase H fold and are encoded in a striking 15% of the available complete prokaryotic genomes. Most of these proteins are encoded in defense islands, often in a close association with known defense systems, hence the designation WARD (Weaponized Antiphage RNase- dependent Defense). The WARDs display a broad variety of protein domain architectures and genomic contexts, including a strong link to restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, retrons, and non-coding RNAs, suggestive of a substantial diversity in defense mechanisms. We experimentally tested 10 WARDs, mostly, encoded by standalone genes, and found that 9 of these conferred robust protection against diverse phages in Escherichia coli. Therefore, WARDs appear to represent the third most abundant defense system type in prokaryotes.

papers.title: Non-homologous end-joining is implicated in rapid and efficient caspofungin adaptation in Nakaseomyces glabratus
papers.abstract: Antifungal resistance in Nakaseomyces glabratus is a major clinical challenge, yet the cellular processes that shape its evolution remain poorly understood. Here, we used experimental evolution to investigate the role of the error-prone double-strand break repair pathway, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), in adaptation to fluconazole and caspofungin. Wild-type and NHEJ-deficient (lig4{Delta}) populations were evolved under antifungal selection for 25 days. Fluconazole resistance emerged rapidly in both genetic backgrounds and was associated with recurrent PDR1 mutations and aneuploidies. In contrast, caspofungin adaptation was delayed and less efficient in lig4{Delta} populations, with several lineages failing to survive. All wild-type caspofungin-evolved isolates carried canonical FKS2 hotspot mutations, whereas lig4{Delta} isolates predominantly acquired resistance through alternative genetic pathways. Caspofungin adaptation also frequently conferred cross-resistance to fluconazole and was accompanied by changes in the abundance of ergosterol-associated proteins. Together, these findings implicate NHEJ in promoting efficient evolution of FKS-mediated echinocandin resistance and demonstrate that DNA repair capacity can shape antifungal resistance trajectories in N. glabratus.

papers.title: Metagenome-assembled genomes reveal water-mass-associated distribution ecotypes of marine Archaea in the Western Arctic Ocean
papers.abstract: Archaea are important contributors to marine biogeochemical cycling, yet their ecology remains poorly characterized in the Arctic Ocean. The three dominant marine archaeal lineages, Marine Groups I, II, and III (MG-I, MG-II, and MG-III), are generally reported to have distinct, clade-consistent vertical distributions that are attributed to light penetration and temperature. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing of seawater collected during the 2015 U.S. Arctic GEOTRACES expedition (GN01) to recover archaeal metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from the Western Arctic Ocean and to relate their relative abundances to water mass structure. Temperature, salinity, silicate, and N* distinguished four water mass layers: the summer surface layer, the Polar Mixed Layer, Atlantic Water, and Arctic Ocean basin water. Of 155 MAGs recovered from a metagenomic co-assembly, 17 were archaeal and represented all three marine groups (four MG-I, eleven MG-II, and two MG-III). Abundance-based clustering of samples from two deep central Arctic stations separated microbial communities according to water mass. Mapping MAG relative abundance across several hundred samples revealed surface, mid-depth, and deep distribution ecotypes; members of every marine group displayed more than one ecotype, and ecotype was not consistent with MAG phylogeny. These results indicate that archaeal distributions in the Western Arctic Ocean are more closely tied to water mass stratification than to clade identity, and that previously reported clade-specific depth distributions of marine Archaea may partly reflect the limited resolution of amplicon-based surveys and shallow sampling.

papers.title: Knockdown of fibrillarin reveals cell- and virus- dependent restriction of henipavirus replication and enhanced antiviral immune signalling
papers.abstract: The henipavirus genus includes several highly pathogenic zoonotic viruses that lack medical countermeasures. The 2-O-methyltransferase fibrillarin (FBL) has been identified by genome-wide functional genomics studies as a henipavirus pro-viral factor. While FBL is a potential target for host-directed antiviral therapeutics, its impact on henipavirus replication in cell types relevant to henipavirus disease has not been explored. Here we demonstrate that depleting cellular FBL using short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) has varying impacts on henipavirus replication, depending on cell type and virus. FBL depletion in small airway epithelial cells (HSAEC1-KT) significantly impaired viral gene transcription for Hendra virus (HeV) genotypes 1 and 2 (HeV-g1, HeV-g2), and Nipah virus (NiV) Bangladesh strain (NiV-B), but not NiV Malaysia (NiV-M) strain or Cedar virus (CedV). Conversely, reduced FBL expression in bronchial epithelial (NuLi-1) cells, aortic endothelial (Telo HAEC) cells or neuroblastoma (BE(2)-M17) cells did not inhibit HeV-g1 replication. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that impaired virus replication in FBL knockdown cells was associated with enhanced activation of innate immune pathways and robust upregulation of interferon stimulated genes (ISGs). Together, these findings demonstrate a virus- and cell-type dependent impact of FBL on henipavirus replication and support a role for FBL in modulation of the antiviral innate immune response.

papers.title: GMP-Cor: Quantifying Transcriptional Dysregulation in Antibiotic Tolerance and Persistence
papers.abstract: When cells are exposed to stress, they typically activate stress-response pathways and enter a regulated growth-arrest. But what if the stress overwhelms these pathways? In such cases, cells may enter a disrupted growth-arrest - a poorly adapted, abrupt cessation of growth, characterized by a broad distribution of lag times upon stress removal. This distribution underlies antibiotic persistence during stress recovery. Therefore, gaining a deeper understanding of the disrupted growth-arrest is important for developing more effective antibiotic therapies. In this study, we perform single cell RNA-seq on bacteria in disrupted conditions. We develop GMP-Cor: a metric to quantify dysregulation and analyze gene-gene correlation patterns in sparse single-cell data. We find that gene-gene correlations are significantly reduced in disrupted cells compared to regulated cells, providing direct evidence that this tolerance-enhanced state, along with its increased membrane sensitivity, is associated with global-dysregulation. We demonstrate that GMP-Cor can extend to other biological systems, such as persistent cancer cells, where it separates proliferating from drug-arrested cells.

papers.title: Description of Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov. from invasive garlic mustard highlights agricultural biosecurity risks of foreign weeds as pathogen reservoirs
papers.abstract: Invasive weeds can increase agricultural biosecurity risks by serving as reservoirs for emerging or undercharacterized plant pathogens. Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata), an invasive brassicaceous weed in North America, occurs near agricultural landscapes and is susceptible to multiple crop pathogens. A previously undescribed Alternaria species was isolated from a diseased garlic mustard population in Maryland, USA, prompting investigation of its taxonomy, origins, and host range. De novo genome sequencing produced a near-chromosome scale assembly of 35.8 Mb comprising 17 contigs. Comparative genomic analyses with other crucifer-infecting Alternaria species revealed expanded repertoires of predicted CAZymes and peptidases, as well as unique effectors and biosynthetic gene clusters. Phylogenetic and comparative analyses supported recognition of this fungus as Alternaria kierstenii sp. nov., representing a distinct lineage within section Sonchi. Host range assays demonstrated that A. kierstenii was highly aggressive on diverse hosts in the Brassicaceae, including vegetable, ornamental, cover crop, and invasive species. The disease caused by this new pathogen manifested as foliar and stem lesions, chlorosis, necrosis, leaf death, and, in several hosts, rapid plant mortality. Amplicon sequence data from a nationwide garlic mustard microbiome study detected closely related taxa only in the plants from the eastern states of Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New York, suggesting a geographically restricted population consistent with expectations for a potentially emerging pathogen. The description of this phylogenetically unique, broad host range pathogen demonstrates the potential for widespread invasive weeds to harbor pathogens and pathogen genomic diversity with agricultural relevance, underscoring the hidden biosecurity risk of understudied invasive weeds.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-associated adaptability of suckermouth catfish inhabiting the polluted Buriganga River: insights into heavy-metal-remediating microorganisms
papers.abstract: The suckermouth catfish (SMCF), known for its pollutant tolerance and high invasiveness, is prevalent in the heavily contaminated Buriganga River in Bangladesh. This waterway, contaminated with a variety of pollutants, including heavy metals, has experienced the near-complete disappearance of native fish populations; however, the suckermouth catfish demonstrates remarkable adaptability in this environment. One objective of this study is to elucidate the role of the gut microbiome in SMCFs' adaptation to this severely polluted habitat. We performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) of gut contents from SMCFs to analyze the gut microbial profiles of the fish samples. The results indicated that the suckermouth catfish's gut is enriched with microbial communities, including Paraclostridium, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus, Bacillus, and Pseudomonas, which have the potential to remediate pollutants, including heavy metals. The subsequent aim of this research is to isolate and identify bacteria from the SMCF gut capable of remediating multiple heavy metals. We isolated three isolates with the potential to remediate multiple heavy metals and identified them as Staphylococcus pasteuri SD, Morganella morganii SAS1, and Sporosarcina saromensis SAS using partial 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and conventional techniques. All isolates showed distinct capabilities for remediating multiple heavy metals. Notably, S. pasteuri showed the highest lead (Pb) bioaccumulation (36.28%), S. saromensis showed the highest chromium (Cr) uptake (39.22%), and M. morganii showed the highest nickel (Ni) uptake (35.90%). Furthermore, these isolates exhibited remarkable metal-tolerance profiles, with maximum tolerable concentrations ranging from 125 ppm to 1000 ppm, and sustained healthy growth under metal-supplemented conditions throughout a 48-hour incubation period. This validates their potential to remediate multiple heavy metals. Collectively, the results underscore the ecological adaptability of suckermouth catfish in polluted aquatic environments, which is associated with their gut microbiome, and highlight the bioremediation potential of these gut-derived microbes as effective agents for mitigating heavy metal contamination.

papers.title: Chromosomally-Encoded Hok/Sok Toxin/Antitoxin SystemsInhibit Phage Infection
papers.abstract: The primary physiological role of toxin/antitoxin (TA) systems is phage defense; they are also used to stabilize mobile genetic elements. In the initial publication in 1996, plasmid-encoded Hok/Sok, a type I TA system (protein toxin, RNA antitoxin that inhibits toxin mRNA), was shown to inhibit T4 phage infection in Escherichia coli by reducing its efficiency of plating and burst size and by increasing the time for mature phage to form (latent period). This publication also identified that the mechanism of Hok/Sok inhibiting T4 was host transcription shutoff, arguably the most-general phage inhibition system since most phages impair host transcription. However, recently, the role of Hok/Sok in phage inhibition has been challenged. Therefore, here we investigated the role of four E. coli chromosomally-expressed, hok+/sok+ loci and the one orphan hok+ locus and found that the Hok proteins inhibit the infection of E. coli by BASEL phage 48, a Vequintavirus with myovirus morphology. Of the five Hok proteins, the greatest phage inhibition was by HokB, and infection by BASEL phages 34 and 39 were also inhibited by HokB. We also find BASEL phage 48 requires the WecB-generated receptor NGR for infection. Therefore, chromosomally-derived orphan Hok proteins, produced at physiological levels, are relevant for phage inhibition.

papers.title: GENOME ASSEMBLIES FOR 28 PHAEOSPHAERIACEAE ISOLATES FROM CANADA
papers.abstract: Glume blotch and Septoria Tritici Blotch (STB) are destructive crop diseases caused by fungal pathogens formerly classified under the genus Septoria. Recent taxonomical revisions have led to the reclassification and renaming of these fungi, some of which are now under the genus Parastagonospora, family Phaeosphaeriaceae, order Pleosporales, and class Dothideomycetes. In this study, we performed whole genome sequencing and assembly for 28 Phaeosphaeriaceae isolates from Canada. Sequencing was performed using a combination of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read and Illumina short-read sequencing platforms. Most of the genomes were very complete, BUSCO >99%, with the genomes assemblies derived from ONT sequencing having very few contigs that likely encompass entire chromosomes or chromosome arms. To determine the relationship between these isolates and similar fungi that have been previously characterized, we performed whole genome alignments to 2,668 other Dothidiomycete genomes obtained from NCBI using NUCmer. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that 27 of the isolates clustered discretely with either Parastagonospora nodorum, or Parastagonospora pseudonodorum (Parastagonospora avenae f. sp. tritici), with one genome having no other similar genome in NCBI which we hypothesize to be the first genome assembly of Phaeosphaeria pontiformis. Both P. nodorum and P. pseudonodorum species were isolated from wheat and barley and only the latter was isolated from durum, while the P. pontiformis was isolated from wheat. In summary, we sequenced and assembled the genomes of 28 isolates of Phaeosphaeriaceae spp. from Canada and the genomes add to our foundational knowledge of these plant pathogens and efforts to better understand their diversity.

papers.title: Proteomic signatures of cold adaptation and sponge host adaptation in marine Archaea
papers.abstract: Temperature shapes the biochemistry of microbial proteins, and several amino acid compositional indices have been proposed to detect cold adaptation in microbial proteomes. Whether these indices capture cold adaptation in Archaea, which are abundant in cold marine environments such as the Arctic Ocean, has not been tested. We calculated six amino acid compositional indices (arginine to lysine ratio, acidic residue proportion, aliphatic index, aromaticity, grand average of hydropathicity, and proline residue proportion) across global protein families for 142 Marine Group I (MG-I; Thaumarchaeota) and 146 Euryarchaeota genomes from the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), together with three MG-I metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) recovered from the Western Arctic Ocean. The Arctic MAGs fell within the range of index and phylogenetic distances of the wider MG-I population, and no signature of cold adaptation was detected. Instead, index values differed between the two main MG-I phylogenetic groups and between freshwater and marine genomes, and the Euryarchaeota formed five index-based clusters consistent with phylogeny. A group of 19 MG-I MAGs associated with sea sponges had significantly higher arginine to lysine ratios than other MG-I, differed in the usage of all amino acids except alanine and lysine, and had distinct codon usage and higher GC content; their anomalous placement in the MG-I phylogeny is consistent with long-branch attraction. These results indicate that amino acid compositional indices developed for Bacteria have limited power to detect cold adaptation in Archaea, but reveal strong proteomic signatures associated with host adaptation in sponge-associated Thaumarchaeota.

papers.title: Defining nutrient dependencies of intestinal Klebsiella pneumoniae guides rational probiotic engineering
papers.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of antibiotic-resistant infections, yet the ecological determinants enabling its intestinal expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we combined in vivo transcriptomics and metabolomics to identify carbon sources exploited by K. pneumoniae during colonization of the antibiotic-disrupted gut across strains and dietary contexts. Despite its metabolic breadth, K. pneumoniae consistently exploited a restricted set of substrates, including arabinose, raffinose, oligogalacturonate, arabitol, xylose, and gluconate, that contributed to intestinal fitness, with related metabolic signatures also observed in antibiotic-treated human samples. Guided by these findings, we engineered Escherichia coli Nissle to enhance consumption of these nutrients and assembled a defined consortium, NICHE, designed to reinforce colonization resistance through nutrient competition. NICHE restricted intestinal expansion of multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae in preventive and therapeutic settings, with efficacy influenced by dietary nutrient availability. Together, this work defines exploitable K. pneumoniae nutrient dependencies and a framework for rational probiotic engineering.

papers.title: Oil biodegradation and marine oil snow formation in Arctic seawater microcosms at 4 °C
papers.abstract: Hudson Bay is a sub-Arctic inland sea characterized by seasonal sea-ice cover, which governs marine circulation, biological productivity, and ecosystem structure. In recent decades, the duration of sea-ice cover has declined, resulting in longer ice-free seasons that are expected to elevate marine activity and environmental exposure to anthropogenic disturbances. As such, the potential for oil spill incidents associated with increased marine operations is expected to rise. To understand microbial biodegradation dynamics associated with marine oil snow (MOS), seawater microcosms amended with diesel fuel were incubated at 4 {degrees}C for 6 weeks. We amended all our microcosms with UV-weathered Churchill diesel fuel at 1% (v/v). 16S rRNA sequencing of the incubations revealed a decline in overall microbial diversity and a dramatic increase in specialized oil-degrading taxa, with Pseudomonas and Pseudoalteromonas being the main taxa involved, as both effectively degrade hydrocarbons under ambient and stimulated conditions. Biostimulation with nutrients (NaNO3, KH2PO4) and an alternative dispersant at 0.1% (v/v) resulted in a greater abundance of MOS aggregates and rapid enrichment of oil-degraders. Simple n-alkanes exhibited the highest biodegradation loss relative to complex polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs); however, biostimulation did not substantially enhance their degradation. Additionally, UV weathering resulted in a 22% loss of PAHs, which is three times higher than the UV loss observed for n-alkanes. Biostimulated samples exhibited an elevated transfer of high molecular weight alkanes and PAHs from the oil into the aqueous phase, accompanied by a rapid enrichment of oil-degrading taxa.

papers.title: Marine oil snow formation in microcosm incubations of artificial seawater at 4 °C
papers.abstract: An oil spill in the Arctic would have far-reaching impacts on the environment, the biota, and the Inuit communities that depend on this unique ecosystem for their livelihoods. Due to the rapid retreat of sea ice in the region, the Arctic is becoming more vulnerable to oil spills. Since microorganisms are the first responders to oil contamination, understanding their behavior is critical for designing bioremediation approaches tailored to Arctic conditions. In this study, we conducted microcosm experiments at 4 {degrees}C in the dark to simulate an Arctic oil spill, using crude oil and diesel as hydrocarbon sources. Biostimulation was tested with the addition of nutrients NaNO3 and KH2PO4, and soy lecithin-Tween 80 dissolved in ethanol as an alternative dispersant. Microcosms were placed on tube rollers at 3 rpm to mimic natural wave action and run with appropriate controls to assess microbial community shifts. Our objectives were to characterize the early microbial succession associated with oil degradation and marine oil snow (MOS) formation, and to determine how nutrients, dispersants, oil type (crude vs. diesel), photochemical aging (fresh vs. weathered), and oil concentration influence these processes. We observed that the combined effect of nutrients and dispersant resulted in rapid MOS formation, occurring as early as 30 minutes after the initial setup. Microbial taxa exhibited varying tolerance to different concentrations of the same oil, and the dominant hydrocarbon degraders in fresh diesel treatments were distinctly different from those in weathered diesel. Furthermore, the nutrient-dispersant treatment promoted an earlier succession of oil-degrading taxa compared to nutrient-only or dispersant-only treatments. Together, these results highlight the importance of cold-adapted microbial communities in driving early oil degradation and MOS formation in Arctic waters, and they provide insights relevant to the development of Arctic-specific bioremediation strategies.

papers.title: Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
papers.abstract: Bacteria are essential to marine ecosystems as they remineralize organic matter, cycle carbon, nitrogen, and other key elements, and support higher trophic levels through food webs. The Bering and Chukchi Seas off the coast of Alaska are among the most productive regions in the world, with intense seasonal algal blooms, yet their bacterial communities remain poorly characterized, and the region is warming rapidly as heat transport from the Pacific Ocean increases. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of 181 samples collected on 0.2 {micro}m filters at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) across 62 stations during the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, when sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm. Hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances resolved 11 sample clusters in three divisions, all dominated by Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia. Community structure was related to water mass, salinity, and bloom stage, but not to depth. Clusters ranged from Gammaproteobacteria-dominant, Bacteroidia-poor assemblages in warm and cool Shelf Water (Division A) to Bacteroidia-rich assemblages spanning pre- to post-bloom conditions (Divisions B and C). In distance-based redundancy analysis, temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, nitrate, and fluorescence together explained 14.8% of the variation in community composition, with salinity the strongest contributor. These results indicate that water-mass origin, physicochemical conditions, and bloom stage jointly shape bacterial communities, and that changes in temperature, salinity, and the magnitude and timing of blooms could substantially alter bacterial communities of this Pacific gateway to the Arctic.

papers.title: Open filament tracks drive Bacteroidota gliding motility
papers.abstract: Bacteria of the phylum Bacteroidota glide across surfaces using adhesins that attach to the substratum and are propelled along the cell body by an underlying track. The track is currently thought to form a single closed loop around the cell. Here we use 3D super-resolution tracking of single adhesin molecules in Flavobacterium johnsoniae to characterize adhesin movements in unprecedented detail. Our data overturn multiple aspects of the single closed loop model by showing that adhesins follow non-repeating trajectories that cross, make sharp turns, and exhibit reversals and circular paths. We develop a new model for Bacteroidota gliding in which the track network comprises multiple independently moving, open filaments. This supramolecular organization resembles that of other moving bacterial filaments such as MreB and FtsZ, suggesting that open filaments are a common organising principle in the bacterial cytoskeleton.

papers.title: Proteolytic feedback of quorum sensing promotes infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Quorum sensing (QS) enables bacteria to coordinate collective behaviors in response to population density. However, the mechanisms by which QS circuits are reset or attenuated remain poorly understood. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the LuxR-type transcription factor RhlR controls virulence gene expression at high cell density, requiring both its cognate acyl-homoserine lactone signal and the accessory protein PqsE for full activity. Here, we show that RhlR abundance is actively controlled by ATP-dependent proteolysis through a self-limiting negative feedback loop. We identify an N-terminal degron within RhlR that is protected from protease recognition by PqsE binding and is required for degradation by both the Lon and the ClpP1-ClpP2 protease complex. Removal of this degron stabilizes RhlR, advancing the timing of QS-regulated gene expression, enhancing biofilm formation, imposes a competitive fitness cost in vitro, and reduced virulence in an acute mouse lung infection. Mechanistically, RhlR directly activates transcription of clpP2, encoding a subunit of the protease complex required for its own degradation, establishing a self-limiting negative feedback loop. Disruption of RhlR DNA binding stabilizes the receptor through dual effects on reduced clpP2 expression and increased PqsE availability via the loss of RhlR-dependent repression of pqsE. Together, these findings reveal proteolytic turnover as an underappreciated regulatory layer of QS-activation and establish a mechanism for how receptor turnover may facilitate the transition away from high-cell density states.

papers.title: Helicase family proteins promote antiviral ADP-ribosylation of DNA purines
papers.abstract: DarTG defense systems studied to date contain a DarT1 or DarT2 toxin that blocks phage replication by ADP-ribosylating DNA and a NADAR or macrodomain antitoxin, DarG, that reverses this modification at homeostasis. Here, we identify additional DarTG subfamilies, one of which comprises a DarT3 toxin, an ADP-ribosylhydrolase (ARH)-domain antitoxin, and a helicase family protein, DarH. The Escherichia coli DarHTG3 system confers broad phage defense, requires DarH and, unlike previously characterized DarTG systems, modifies adenine. Characterization of additional DarH-containing DarTG systems reveals that a subset also target guanine. Our data support a model in which ADP-bound DarH functions as a processivity factor by recruiting DarT to its single-stranded DNA substrate and allowing for ADP-ribosylation of multiple target sites. These findings reveal how a helicase family protein regulates an antiviral effector by promoting DNA engagement rather than unwinding and thereby expanding the functional repertoire of helicase family proteins in bacterial immunity.

papers.title: Mucosal ACP subunit vaccine formulated with a small molecule STING agonist drives protective TH1/TH17 responses and serum bactericidal antibodies against Neisseria gonorrhoeae
papers.abstract: STING agonists are emerging vaccine adjuvants; however, only cyclic dinucleotides (low permeability and stability) have been tested against pathogenic bacteria. We examined diABZI, a non-nucleotide STING agonist active in human and murine orthologs, combined with the Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) Adhesin Complex Protein, a conserved adhesin and human lysozyme C inhibitor, as a gonococcal vaccine. Intranasal administration of recombinant ACP (rACP)+diABZI accelerated gonococcal clearance, in contrast to rACP or rACP+CpG+MPLA, despite comparable antibody responses. While both diABZI and CpG+MPLA induced TH1, diABZI also induced TH17 polarization. Peptide mapping localized the immunodominant T cell epitopes to the ACP-lysozyme C interface. rACP+diABZI elicited higher human serum bactericidal activity (hSBA), that correlated with Ng clearance, and antibodies that reversed human lysozyme C inhibition and interfered with Ng adhesion and invasion in 3D human vaginal/urethral mucosal models. Passive serum transfer did not recapitulate protection, implicating mucosal antibodies and cellular immunity over circulating IgG.

papers.title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
papers.abstract: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell-Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 {degrees}C and 20 {degrees}C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas, and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 {degrees}C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.

papers.title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.

papers.title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
papers.abstract: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non-processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP-ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.

papers.title: Draft genome of Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 isolated from marine oil snow in the Churchill Marine Observatory, MB, Canada
papers.abstract: An oil-degrading enrichment culture was inoculated from Marine Oil Snow (MOS) collected during an oil-spill experiment at the Churchill Marine Observatory in winter 2024. The complete metagenome-assembled genome for Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 was reconstructed, exhibiting the genetic potential to degrade hydrocarbons, including alkanes and aromatic compounds, as well as the ability to produce surfactants.

papers.title: Structure of Bacillus cereus ZmaM, a peptidase-ABC transporter that secretes and activates zwittermicin A
papers.abstract: Bacteria engage in microbial warfare by secreting toxic molecules. These toxins can serve as therapeutics or drug discovery starting points, motivating investigations of their production. Bacteria that produce these toxins must protect themselves, and a common strategy is to synthesize an inactive prodrug that is activated upon secretion. Some prodrugs are capped with N-acyl-[x1D05]-asparagine motifs, which are removed by two types of prodrug peptidases. Type I peptidases are membrane-bound S12 hydrolases; type II peptidases have an additional C-terminal half-ABC transporter module. Recent structures of a type I peptidase revealed how its transmembrane domain completes the substrate-binding site, but little is known about type II peptidases. Here, we show that the B. cereus type II peptidase ZmaM is responsible for both the export of prezwittermicin and its activation into zwittermicin. The structure of homodimeric ZmaM reveals a central type IV ABC transporter flanked by peptidase modules. The periplasmic hydrolase domains interact over the transporter's open outer vestibule. Mutations to intermodule interfaces impact both peptidase and ATP hydrolysis activities, indicating the peptidase and transporter modules are interdependent. Together, our findings reveal an evolutionary strategy to coordinate toxin activation with its export and inform future efforts to harness these systems in biotechnology.

papers.title: Genome-wide CRISPRi-seq maps essential-gene contributions to aminoglycoside susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic ESKAPE pathogen whose multiple intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance mechanisms restrict treatment options. Essential genes offer potential antimicrobial targets, but their vulnerability to partial inhibition and contribution to antibiotic susceptibility remain incompletely characterized. Here, we developed a rhamnose-inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) platform and an 83,078-guide library for genome-wide screening in PAO1, with mismatch guides enabling graded repression. Fitness profiling in antibiotic-free Mueller-Hinton medium identified 743 genes whose repression reduced competitive fitness and revealed sequence features associated with guide performance. Combining full-match and mismatch-guide responses revealed substantial variation in essential-gene fitness effects across predicted repression strengths, while comparison of fitness profiles between Mueller-Hinton medium and fetal bovine serum identified condition-dependent effects alongside a conserved fitness landscape. Under aminoglycoside exposure, we identified 118 recurrent sensitizing and 120 recurrent protective gene knockdowns, including many targeting essential and fitness-associated functions. Growth and killing assays with individual strains confirmed that CRISPRi targeting of atpI, accC, secA and ftsZ enhanced tobramycin activity. Finally, transcriptome analysis of these knockdowns confirmed target silencing, captured polar effects on neighboring genes and revealed distinct but overlapping transcriptional responses. Together, these findings quantify the variable fitness costs of essential-gene repression and identify candidate targets for potentiating aminoglycoside activity. IMPORTANCE Essential bacterial genes are difficult to study because their complete disruption prevents growth. Yet knowing that a gene is essential does not reveal how strongly its activity must be reduced to impair growth. Here, we developed a method to examine how reduced gene expression affects fitness across the genome of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a major cause of difficult-to-treat infections. This approach identified essential functions particularly vulnerable to partial depletion and mapped how gene repression alters aminoglycoside susceptibility. Repressing selected genes impaired growth and disproportionately increased killing by tobramycin. These tools and datasets provide a resource for prioritizing candidate antibacterial targets and investigating whether partial inhibition of essential functions can enhance the activity of existing antibiotics.

papers.title: CYP123, a sterol C4-methyl oxidase, acts with CYP51 to initiate mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism
papers.abstract: Mycobacteria exploit host cholesterol, both as a carbon source and as a source of catabolites proposed to modulate host immunity, but their capacity to catabolise other host sterols has not been established. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate of host cholesterol biosynthesis, accumulates in the activated macrophages these bacteria infect. Here we define the initiating steps of mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism, combining genomic enzymology, transcriptional profiling, mutagenesis, biochemistry, NMR and crystallography. We identify the cytochrome P450 CYP123 as a sterol C4-methyl oxidase. It is encoded with the lanosterol 14-demethylase CYP51 in a co-oriented region conserved across most Mycobacteriaceae. The region carries no binding site for the cholesterol-responsive regulators KstR or KstR2, and in M. abscessus lanosterol induces both genes while cholesterol does not. CYP123 oxidises the C4-methyl group of C14-demethylated sterols in three steps to the carboxylic acid, yet acts on neither lanosterol nor cholesterol, because Met82 excludes the C14-methylated precursor. An M82A variant binds and oxidises lanosterol. In a single reaction containing both recombinant M. smegmatis enzymes, CYP51 converts lanosterol to FF-MAS, which CYP123 then oxidises to the C4-carboxylic acid, so the two act in sequence. M. smegmatis, M. phlei and M. abscessus grow on lanosterol as a sole carbon source. Growth slows in M. smegmatis cyp123 and cyp51 mutants. Mycobacterial sterol catabolism therefore extends beyond cholesterol, and blocking the cholesterol route alone may not deprive these organisms of host sterols. Induction where lanosterol confers no growth advantage raises the possibility that the pathway also serves functions beyond carbon acquisition.
